items.prompt: What makes a bird's bones light enough for flight?

options.label: They are hollow inside
options.feedback: Air fills them, and thin struts keep them strong.

options.label: They are made of cartilage
options.feedback: Cartilage bends too easily to carry a flying body.

options.label: They are filled with fat
options.feedback: Fat is fuel, and it is stored in the body, not the bones.

options.label: They are far smaller than ours
options.feedback: An eagle's wing bone is longer than your forearm.

items.ok_line: Hollow bones, braced from within — light without being weak.
items.ko_line: Think about what is inside the bone rather than what it is made of.
items.exp_text: Many of a bird's bones are hollow tubes rather than solid rods. Inside them run thin bony struts, arranged much like the bracing of a bridge, so the bone resists bending without carrying the weight of a solid one. Some of these hollows even connect to the breathing system and hold air. The saving matters: a frigatebird with a two-metre wingspan has a skeleton weighing less than its feathers.

items.prompt: Which part of a bird's chest anchors its flight muscles?

options.label: The keel
options.feedback: A deep blade of bone running down the breastbone.

options.label: The wishbone
options.feedback: It springs with each stroke, but the muscles do not grip it.

options.label: The shoulder blade
options.feedback: It steadies the wing joint rather than powering it.

options.label: The lowest ribs
options.feedback: Ribs protect the organs; they pull nothing.

items.ok_line: The keel is the anchor the whole downstroke pulls against.
items.ko_line: Look for the bone that sticks out like the blade of a boat.
items.exp_title: A blade of bone down the chest
items.exp_text: The breastbone of a flying bird carries a tall ridge called the keel, and the flight muscles are fixed to both its faces. It gives them the broad surface they need to grip. In a pigeon these muscles make up about a fifth of the whole body. Birds that gave up flying, such as the ostrich and the emu, have lost the keel — their breastbone is flat, because nothing pulls on it any more.

items.prompt: Why does air flowing over a wing lift the bird?

options.label: Pressure above the wing drops
options.feedback: Faster air presses down less, so the wing is pushed up.

options.label: The feathers repel the air
options.feedback: Feathers shape the flow; they do not push it away.

options.label: Warm air rises beneath it
options.feedback: That lifts a soaring bird on a thermal, not a flapping one.

options.label: The wing is lighter than air
options.feedback: Nothing about a bird is lighter than the air around it.

items.ok_line: Less push from above than from below, and the wing rises.
items.ko_line: The answer is about pressure, not about weight or warmth.
items.exp_title: A wing is pushed up more than down
items.exp_text: A wing is curved on top and flatter beneath, and it meets the air tilted slightly nose-up. Air passing over the curved upper surface travels faster than the air underneath, and fast-moving air presses less hard. The wing is therefore pushed up from below more than it is pushed down from above, and the difference is lift. Tilt the wing too steeply and the flow breaks away — the bird stalls and drops.

items.prompt: What is the small tuft of feathers on the leading edge of a wing called?

options.label: The alula
options.feedback: A thumb-like tuft that keeps slow flight from collapsing.

options.label: The coverts
options.feedback: These smooth the wing's surface, further back.

options.label: The primaries
options.feedback: The long feathers at the wingtip that bite the air.

options.label: The down
options.feedback: Soft feathers underneath, for warmth rather than flight.

items.ok_line: The alula is a bird's thumb, and it earns its keep on landing.
items.ko_line: It sits at the very front of the wing, and a bird can raise it.
items.exp_title: A thumb that stops the stall
items.exp_text: The alula is a small group of feathers growing from what is left of a bird's thumb, at the front edge of the wing. Flying slowly, a wing tilts steeply and the airflow threatens to break away. Raising the alula opens a narrow slot that sends a fast stream of air across the wing's top and keeps the flow attached. That is why a bird can come in slowly to a branch instead of dropping onto it.

items.prompt: What is a bird's wishbone made from?

options.label: Two fused collarbones
options.feedback: They meet at the front and act as a spring.

options.label: Two fused lower ribs
options.feedback: Ribs stay separate, and they sit further back.

options.label: The tip of the breastbone
options.feedback: That is the keel, and it is a different bone.

options.label: The base of the neck
options.feedback: The neck bones stay free so the head can turn.

items.ok_line: Two collarbones joined into one springy V.
items.ko_line: You have the same pair of bones, but yours are not joined.
items.exp_title: Your collarbones, welded into a spring
items.exp_text: The wishbone is the two collarbones fused into a single V at the front of the chest. It is not merely a brace. High-speed film shows it bending apart on the downstroke and springing back on the up, storing and returning energy at every beat, and helping to pump air through the chest. Dinosaurs close to the ancestors of birds already had one, long before any of them left the ground.

items.prompt: How does air travel through a bird's lungs?

options.label: In one direction only
options.feedback: Air sacs push it through in a loop, never back.

options.label: Back and forth as in ours
options.feedback: That is a mammal's way, and it wastes each breath.

options.label: Only while the bird glides
options.feedback: Breathing never stops, gliding or not.

options.label: Through the hollow bones alone
options.feedback: Bones hold air, but they are not where it is used.

items.ok_line: One-way flow, so fresh air reaches the lungs on every stroke.
items.ko_line: A bird's breath does not reverse the way yours does.
items.exp_title: A one-way loop, not a bellows
items.exp_text: Your lungs fill and empty along the same path, so each breath in is diluted by the stale air left behind. A bird instead has air sacs before and behind the lungs that drive air through them in one direction. Fresh air crosses the lungs while breathing in and again while breathing out. This is why bar-headed geese can cross the Himalayas at heights where a climber can barely move.

options.label: The hummingbird
options.feedback: Its wing traces a figure of eight and reverses at will.

options.label: The swift
options.feedback: Fast and tireless forwards, but it cannot back up.

options.label: The kingfisher
options.feedback: It hovers before a dive, then goes only one way: down.

options.label: The barn owl
options.feedback: Silent and slow, but never in reverse.

items.ok_line: The only bird that can hold still, go up, and go back.
items.ko_line: Think of the bird that hangs motionless in front of a flower.
items.exp_title: A wing that works on both strokes
items.exp_text: Most birds get lift on the downstroke and simply recover on the up. A hummingbird twists its wing almost upside down at the top of each beat, so both strokes push air and the bird stays where it is. Change the tilt and the same motion carries it backwards or straight up. It beats its wings around fifty times a second, which is why they blur, and why the sound is a hum.

items.prompt: Which wing shape suits a bird that must turn sharply among trees?

options.label: Short and rounded
options.feedback: Slow, but it turns inside a gap between branches.

options.label: Long and narrow
options.feedback: Built for hours over open sea, not for corners.

options.label: Long and pointed
options.feedback: That shape is for speed in a straight line.

options.label: Broad and flat
options.feedback: Good for riding rising air over open ground.

items.ok_line: A short wing turns tightly, which is what a wood demands.
items.ko_line: A long wing cannot swing round without hitting something.
items.exp_title: The wood asks for a short wing
items.exp_text: Wing shape follows the life a bird leads. Short, rounded wings give quick take-off and tight turns, which is what a sparrowhawk needs weaving between trunks. Long, narrow wings suit the albatross, which locks them out and rides ocean wind for hours. Long, pointed wings belong to the falcon in a dive. None of these is better than another; each is the answer to a different question.

items.prompt: How does an albatross cross an ocean with almost no flapping?

options.label: It rides the wind's changing speed
options.feedback: Climbing and diving between fast and slow air.

options.label: It glides slowly downhill
options.feedback: A pure glide would reach the water within minutes.

options.label: It floats on warm rising air
options.feedback: Thermals rise over land, and it flies over cold sea.

options.label: It is carried by ocean spray
options.feedback: Spray wets feathers; it does not hold up a bird.

items.ok_line: It takes its energy from the wind, not from its muscles.
items.ko_line: The answer lies in how wind speed changes just above the waves.
items.exp_title: Free energy in a layered wind
items.exp_text: Just above the waves the wind is slowed by the water; a few metres higher it runs much faster. An albatross climbs into the fast layer, turns downwind, dives back into the slow one, and turns again, gaining a little speed on every cycle. It can hold this for hours with its wings locked by a tendon, and its heart beats barely faster than at rest. Some birds circle the whole Southern Ocean this way.

items.prompt: Why do many large birds fly in a V?

options.label: Each rides the air the bird ahead stirs
options.feedback: The wingtip leaves rising air, and the next bird sits in it.

options.label: It keeps the flock warmer
options.feedback: They are too far apart to share any heat.

options.label: It hides them from hunters below
options.feedback: A V is one of the easiest shapes to spot.

options.label: It lets the leader hear the others
options.feedback: Calls carry in any formation they choose.

items.ok_line: Every bird but the leader is getting a lift for free.
items.ko_line: The reason has to do with the air left behind a wingtip.
items.exp_title: Sitting in someone else's rising air
items.exp_text: A wingtip leaves a swirl behind it, and just outside that swirl the air is rising. A bird placed there gets part of its lift for nothing and can save something like a fifth of its effort. Ibises fitted with recorders were found to hold the right spot and even to time their wingbeats to the swirl. The lead bird gains least, which is why the front place is handed round during a long flight.
